title: The Constitution of India — An Introduction

learn.hook: India's Constitution was not written in a day. Hundreds of members debated it for nearly three years before signing it by hand!
points: A constitution is the basic rulebook of a country. It sets up the government, divides its powers and protects the rights of citizens.
The Constituent Assembly, which wrote India's Constitution, first met on 9 December 1946. Dr Rajendra Prasad was elected its President.
Dr B. R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee, which prepared the draft. He is often called the chief architect of the Constitution.
The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 (now Constitution Day, or Samvidhan Divas) and came into force on 26 January 1950 (Republic Day). It took nearly three years to make.

The Assembly included members from many regions and communities, including 15 women such as Sarojini Naidu, Hansa Mehta, Durgabai Deshmukh and Ammu Swaminathan. The original copies were handwritten and decorated by artists led by Nandalal Bose.

example.q: Why was 26 January chosen as the day the Constitution would come into force?
steps: On 26 January 1930, Indian freedom fighters had pledged to work for Pūrṇa Swarāj (complete independence).
Leaders wanted to honour that pledge.
So the Constitution, adopted in November 1949, was brought into force on 26 January 1950.
example.answer: To honour the Pūrṇa Swarāj pledge made on 26 January 1930.

learn.reallife: Every year on Republic Day, the parade in New Delhi celebrates the day our Constitution came into force; schools celebrate Constitution Day on 26 November.

A woman member of the Constituent Assembly

quiz.q: When did the Constituent Assembly first meet?
quiz.explain: The Assembly's first meeting was on 9 December 1946.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the key dates of the Constitution

quiz.q: Who chaired the Drafting Committee of the Constitution?
quiz.explain: Dr Ambedkar led the committee that prepared the draft.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the Drafting Committee chairman with the Assembly President

quiz.q: Who was the President of the Constituent Assembly?
quiz.explain: Dr Rajendra Prasad presided over the Assembly and later became India's first President.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the two key roles

quiz.q: On which day was the Constitution adopted?
quiz.explain: It was adopted on 26 November 1949, now celebrated as Constitution Day.
quiz.mistake: Confuses adoption with coming into force

quiz.q: Republic Day, 26 January, marks the day when:
options: The Constitution came into force in 1950
quiz.explain: On 26 January 1950, the Constitution came into force and India became a republic.
quiz.mistake: Confuses Republic Day with Independence Day

quiz.q: About how long did it take to make the Constitution?
quiz.explain: From December 1946 to November 1949: nearly three years of debate and drafting.
quiz.mistake: Underestimates the work involved

quiz.q: How many women were members of the Constituent Assembly?
quiz.explain: Fifteen women, including Sarojini Naidu and Hansa Mehta, were members.
quiz.mistake: Assumes there were no or very few women

quiz.q: What is a constitution?
options: The basic rulebook of a country
quiz.explain: It sets up the government, divides powers and protects citizens' rights.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a constitution is an ordinary book or law

teach.ask: Gappu asks how India's Constitution was made. Tell him the story.
teach.praise: An Assembly, Dr Ambedkar's committee, and two special dates. Now I know why we celebrate Republic Day!
teach.nudge: Good! When was it adopted, and when did it come into force?

learn.hook: The Preamble is like the first page of a promise: it tells us who made the Constitution and what kind of country India wants to be.
points: The Preamble begins with 'We, the people of India', showing that the Constitution draws its power from the people.
It declares India to be a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic. The words 'socialist' and 'secular' were added in 1976 by the 42nd Amendment.

Sovereign: India makes its own decisions. Secular: the State treats all religions equally and has no official religion. Democratic: people elect their government. Republic: the head of the state is elected, not a hereditary ruler.

It promises citizens Justice (social, economic and political), Liberty (of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship), Equality (of status and opportunity) and Fraternity (a feeling of brotherhood and sisterhood).
Fraternity assures the dignity of every individual and the unity and integrity of the nation.

example.q: India's President is elected, not born into the job. Which word in the Preamble does this fact show?
steps: A republic is a country where the head of the state is elected.
India's head of state, the President, is elected.
So India is a republic, not a monarchy.

learn.reallife: Many schools have students read the Preamble aloud in the morning assembly to remember these shared values.

games.title: Preamble words
pairs: All religions are treated equally by the State

games.title: Preamble: true or false?
items: The Preamble begins with 'We, the people of India'.
This shows the people are the source of the Constitution's authority.
The word 'secular' was in the Preamble from 1950.
'Socialist' and 'secular' were added in 1976.
Liberty in the Preamble includes liberty of thought and expression.
It promises liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship.
A republic has a hereditary king as head of state.
In a republic, the head of state is elected.
Equality in the Preamble includes equality of opportunity.
It promises equality of status and of opportunity.
Justice in the Preamble is social, economic and political.
These are the three kinds of justice it names.

quiz.q: With which words does the Preamble begin?
quiz.explain: It begins 'We, the people of India', showing that power comes from the people.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the Constitution comes from rulers or institutions

quiz.q: Which two words were added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment in 1976?
quiz.explain: 'Socialist' and 'secular' were added in 1976.
quiz.mistake: Does not know which words were added later

quiz.q: 'Secular' in the Preamble means:
options: The State treats all religions equally and has no official religion
The State is run by priests
quiz.explain: A secular State respects all religions equally and does not favour any.
quiz.mistake: Confuses secular with anti-religious or theocratic

quiz.q: India is called a 'republic' because:
options: The head of the state is elected
quiz.explain: In a republic, the head of state is chosen, not born into the position.
quiz.mistake: Confuses republic with democracy or monarchy

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four values Justice, Liberty, Equality and Fraternity?
quiz.explain: The Preamble promises justice, liberty, equality and fraternity, not wealth.
quiz.mistake: Adds an attractive word that is not in the Preamble

quiz.q: 'Fraternity' means:
options: A feeling of brotherhood and sisterhood among all
quiz.explain: Fraternity is the spirit of togetherness that assures dignity and unity.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up fraternity with liberty or democracy

quiz.q: 'Sovereign' means that India:
options: Makes its own decisions without outside control
quiz.explain: A sovereign country is independent and decides its own internal and external matters.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the meaning of sovereign

quiz.q: The Preamble promises liberty of:
options: Thought, expression, belief, faith and worship
quiz.explain: Liberty in the Preamble is about freedom of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship, within the law.
quiz.mistake: Thinks liberty means doing anything at all

teach.ask: Gappu found a page called the Preamble. Explain what it says about India.
teach.praise: We, the people, made a promise of justice, liberty, equality and fraternity. That's a beautiful promise!
teach.nudge: Good! What values does the Preamble promise to every citizen?

topics.title: Rights, duties and the spirit of the Constitution

learn.hook: Rights are like the shield the Constitution gives you; duties are what you give back to the country.
points: The Constitution gives every citizen Fundamental Rights: the Right to Equality, Right to Freedom, Right against Exploitation, Right to Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights, and the Right to Constitutional Remedies.
The Right to Constitutional Remedies lets a citizen go to court if their rights are violated. Dr Ambedkar called it the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution.
Fundamental Duties were added in 1976. They include respecting the Constitution, the national flag and the national anthem, protecting the environment, and protecting public property.

The Constitution of India is the longest written constitution in the world. It can be amended (changed) by Parliament, but in the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) the Supreme Court held that its basic structure cannot be changed.
It sets up a federal system with a Union government and State governments, and a separate, independent judiciary.

example.q: A child aged 12 is made to work all day in a factory instead of going to school. Which Fundamental Right protects this child?
steps: Making a young child work in a factory is exploitation.
The Constitution bans employing children below 14 in factories, mines and hazardous work.
This is part of the Right against Exploitation.

learn.reallife: When you keep your park clean or do not scribble on a public bus, you are doing a Fundamental Duty: protecting public property and the environment.

games.title: Right or duty?
items: Equality before the law
Freedom of speech
Going to court if rights are violated
Respecting the national flag
Protecting the environment
Protecting public property
Freedom to follow one's religion

games.title: Which right?
pairs: Everyone is equal before the law
Going to court to protect rights
Freedom to follow and practise one's faith

quiz.q: How many Fundamental Rights does the Constitution list today?
quiz.explain: There are six: Equality, Freedom, against Exploitation, Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational, and Constitutional Remedies.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the number of rights with the number of duties

quiz.q: Which Fundamental Right did Dr Ambedkar call the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution?
quiz.explain: Without the right to go to court, other rights could not be protected.
quiz.mistake: Picks the most familiar right

quiz.q: Fundamental Duties were added to the Constitution in:
quiz.explain: They were added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976.
quiz.mistake: Assumes they were there from the start

quiz.q: Which of these is a Fundamental Duty?
options: Right to vote in every election
quiz.explain: Protecting public property is a duty; the others are rights.
quiz.mistake: Confuses rights with duties

quiz.q: The Right against Exploitation protects children from:
options: Being made to work in factories and hazardous jobs
quiz.explain: Children below 14 cannot be employed in factories, mines or hazardous work.
quiz.mistake: Does not link child labour with this right

quiz.q: In which case did the Supreme Court say that the basic structure of the Constitution cannot be changed?
quiz.explain: In the Kesavananda Bharati case, the Court ruled that Parliament cannot change the basic structure.
quiz.mistake: Does not know this landmark case

quiz.q: Which statement about India's Constitution is correct?
options: It can never be changed at all
It has no rights for citizens
It is the longest written constitution in the world
It was written in one week
quiz.explain: It is very detailed and is the longest written constitution; it can be amended, but not its basic structure.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the Constitution cannot be amended at all

quiz.q: If a person's Fundamental Right is violated, they can:
quiz.explain: The Right to Constitutional Remedies lets citizens approach the courts.
quiz.mistake: Does not know how rights are protected

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know what rights he would have as a citizen, and what duties too.
teach.praise: Rights to protect me, duties to give back, and courts to help. That's fair!
teach.nudge: Good! Can you also tell me about the duties, or what to do if a right is taken away?
